I am 72 years old, and I have farmed these fields in Quzhou since I was a young man following my father. My bones ache more than they used to, and I don't have the strength for crops that demand constant attention like cotton with its endless spraying. I have five mu of good land, and I know every inch of it. This year, just like every year I can remember, I will stick to the winter wheat–summer maize rotation. My wheat went in last October before the ground froze, and now that spring has arrived, it is greening up. I will irrigate it four times total—once now at green-up, again at jointing, at heading, and finally at grain-filling. I top-dress with urea at green-up and heading because the wheat is hungry then. I use improved wheat seed from the county supply store; I stopped saving my own seed years ago when I saw the yield fall. In the autumn, I do rotary tillage to loosen the soil before sowing, but for the summer maize after wheat harvest in early June, I plant directly into the stubble with no-tillage. It saves diesel, time, and my back. Maize only needs two good irrigations—at jointing and at grain-filling. I buy hybrid maize seed, usually something like Nongda 372. For both crops, I apply compound fertilizer as a base and watch the plants to see if they need more. I spray for weeds once, insects twice, and for wheat I add one fungicide spray because the damp spring brings disease. I expect about 500 kg per mu of wheat and 600 kg per mu of maize. It is not a gamble; it is what this land has given me for fifty years, and at my age, I do not gamble.
